title: Reading History and Selection from Genomes
endLine: Neutral change sets the baseline; departures hint at selection or gene flow.

scenes.tts: How can genomes date splits that left no fossil, and spot selection? Our species arose in Africa, yet people with ancestry outside Africa carry a little Neanderthal D N A. Genomes record history in variants, the sites where they differ.
scenes.caption: How can genomes date splits that left no fossil, and spot selection? Our species arose in Africa, yet people with ancestry outside Africa carry a little Neanderthal DNA. Genomes record history in variants, the sites where they differ.
scenes.visual: Open directly on our carried evolutionary canvas (schematic, dark slate background, subject filling most of the frame height): top half holds a glowing branching tree with a brief question banner ('Date splits from DNA?') fading in right at the start; bottom half holds aligned horizontal genome strips (no molecular structures) with no date stamp on them. As 'Africa' and 'Neanderthal DNA' are spoken, a faint connecting thread briefly pulses from a side Neanderthal branch into an out-of-Africa branch, and bright vertical ticks light up along the genome strips to mark 'Variants'.
scenes.narration: How can genomes date splits that left no fossil, and spot selection? Our species arose in Africa, yet people with ancestry outside Africa carry a little Neanderthal DNA. Genomes record history in variants, the sites where they differ.

scenes.tts: Start with neutral changes, variants with no effect on survival or reproduction. On average, they become substitutions at the rate they arise, whatever the population size. So the substitution rate, K, equals the mutation rate, mu. Neutral differences pile up steadily, and one dated split turns their count into years.

scenes.visual: Carry the same tree and aligned genome strips, focusing cleanly on two splitting species branches (schematic). Softly glowing neutral ticks appear at steady intervals along both strips as time moves downward along a left-hand vertical time axis; as the rates are named, a crisp high-contrast readout writes 'K (substitution rate) = mu (mutation rate)' on the right while a steady tick counter rises smoothly. When 'one dated split' is spoken, a single anchor marker locks onto the branch fork and illuminates year-scale ticks along the time axis (schematic).

scenes.tts: Over long spans, a site can change twice, hiding the first change. So observed difference p is corrected into distance D. For small p the correction is tiny. At p of zero point three zero, D is zero point three eight three. D over p is about one point two eight: over a quarter more change.
scenes.caption: Over long spans, a site can change twice, hiding the first change. So observed difference p is corrected into distance D. For small p the correction is tiny. At p of 0.30, D is 0.383. D ÷ p is about 1.28: over a quarter more change.
scenes.visual: Zoom gently into one aligned genome strip pair from the carried world (schematic): an already-coloured variant tick flashes and overwrites itself with a new colour, showing a hidden second change at the same site. In the right readout zone, bar pairs grow as spoken (computed from given numbers): first p = 0.012 beside D = 0.0121 (nearly identical heights, appearing on 'small p'); then p = 0.30 beside D = 0.383. Then 'D ÷ p = 0.383 ÷ 0.30 ≈ 1.28' writes on screen as spoken, and the extra gap above p lights in an accent colour.

scenes.tts: Departures from this neutral baseline are clues to selection, or to gene flow, genes moving between populations by mating. Ancient D N A, from bones tens of thousands of years old, is compared with living genomes. Place four genomes on one tree: African, Eurasian, Neanderthal, and a chimpanzee outgroup. The outgroup marks each site's older version, allele A.

The outgroup marks each site's older version, allele A.
scenes.visual: Transform the carried two-branch tree smoothly into a four-tip population tree (schematic): Chimpanzee on the far outside branch ('Outgroup'), Neanderthal branching next, and African and Eurasian paired as closest sisters. Beneath the four tips sit four aligned horizontal genome strips; a warm bone-to-strip glow draws in the Neanderthal strip as 'Ancient DNA' is spoken. Highlight a column of sites starting from the Chimpanzee strip, stamping high-contrast 'A' markers downward as the ancestral allele.

scenes.tts: Call a newer, derived variant B, and check sites where the Neanderthal carries B. On this tree, the African and Eurasian are each other's closest relatives. Without later gene flow from Neanderthals, which living genome should share B more often?
scenes.caption: Call a newer, derived variant B, and check sites where the Neanderthal carries B. On this tree, the African and Eurasian are each other's closest relatives. Without later gene flow from Neanderthals, which living genome should share B more often?
scenes.visual: Keep the exact four-genome tree and aligned strips on screen (schematic). Flip highlighted newer variants on the Neanderthal strip to bright 'B' markers and dim all other columns so only Neanderthal-B sites remain active. Pulse the sister fork linking African and Eurasian, then raise a clean high-contrast question card at the top: 'Without gene flow, who shares B more?' beside two empty waiting tally bars for African and Eurasian on the right.
scenes.narration: Call a newer, derived variant B, and check sites where the Neanderthal carries B. On this tree, the African and Eurasian are each other's closest relatives. Without later gene flow from Neanderthals, which living genome should share B more often?

scenes.visual: Hold the four-genome tree, Neanderthal-B columns, empty African and Eurasian tally bars, and top question banner ('Without gene flow, who shares B more?') on screen (schematic). Only slow ambient motion plays: Neanderthal B markers shimmer gently while a clean progress bar fills steadily along the bottom edge for the duration of the pause.

scenes.tts: Without gene flow, neither should win. Both reach the Neanderthal only through the same shared ancestor. Yet people with ancestry in Europe or Asia carry a little Neanderthal D N A. That is past gene flow. Patterns can mislead, though.
scenes.caption: Without gene flow, neither should win. Both reach the Neanderthal only through the same shared ancestor. Yet people with ancestry in Europe or Asia carry a little Neanderthal DNA. That is past gene flow. Patterns can mislead, though.
scenes.visual: On the same four-genome canvas (schematic), the question banner clears and both African and Eurasian tally bars first rise to equal dashed baseline levels while the single shared branch linking the African–Eurasian pair to the Neanderthal fork pulses. Then the Eurasian tally bar rises a little above the dashed baseline (schematic, no counts) as a thin glowing bridge connects the Neanderthal and Eurasian branches.
scenes.narration: Without gene flow, neither should win. Both reach the Neanderthal only through the same shared ancestor. Yet people with ancestry in Europe or Asia carry a little Neanderthal DNA. That is past gene flow. Patterns can mislead, though.

scenes.tts: The clock requires one steady rate across the dated split and the target. Real substitutions arrive irregularly. Slightly harmful mutations break the clock, because their rate depends on population size. Even the sequence tree is an inference with stated support. So a departure from neutral counts is a clue to selection, not proof.

scenes.visual: Keep the carried tree and strips (schematic) and show each caution in place: the steady time-axis ticks jitter irregularly as 'arrive irregularly' is spoken; one branch thickens and narrows to represent changing effective population size while amber ticks slow and speed up; a branch node briefly softens with a support badge to show the tree is inferred. On the right readout, an upward spike above the neutral baseline gets labelled 'Clue, not proof'.

scenes.tts: Until the early 1990s, many researchers favored multiregional evolution: regional populations each becoming our species. Living and ancient genomes now strongly support an African origin. Living people trace most ancestry to African populations. And people with ancestors outside Africa carry a little Neanderthal D N A.

scenes.visual: On the carried tree (schematic), faint parallel regional stems labelled 'Multiregional (favored to early 1990s)' dissolve and reform into a braided African-origin tree with living branches tracing most ancestry back to Africa. A thin glowing thread from the ancient Neanderthal branch feeds into the out-of-Africa branch ('a little Neanderthal DNA').

scenes.tts: Proof of selection needs other evidence, like field records. Boag and Grant, in 1981, compared survivors of the 1977 drought on Daphne Major with the banded population beforehand. Larger birds, especially males with larger beaks, survived best. Beak and body size go together, so survival alone cannot name the target. Neutral baselines turn departures into testable clues.

scenes.visual: Transition smoothly within the right readout and lower zone (schematic) from the genomic 'Clue, not proof' meter to a before-and-after field comparison labelled 'Field record: Daphne Major, 1977' and 'Boag & Grant, 1981': clean bird silhouettes (no clutter) shift toward larger body and beak size among survivors, with a linked bracket tying 'Beak size' and 'Body size' together to show they go together. Finally, the full carried tree and neutral baseline glow calmly behind the readout.
